content:
Support has collected these reports about people joining and leaving workspaces:

1. A contractor who was removed from a workspace last year was invited again this week. Clicking the invite link ends in "Something went wrong"; the person is not listed as a member and cannot get in.
2. New people who accept an invitation cannot do anything afterwards: every page tells them they are not a member of the workspace, even though the members page lists them. That workspace also reports fewer seats in use than it has people listed, and invitations keep being accepted long after the plan's seats should have run out.
3. Invitees who open their link the next morning are told it has expired.
4. A workspace with two people on a three-seat plan cannot invite anyone: "all seats are taken". Its invitations page only shows invitations that expired weeks ago, and the owner has revoked several more.
5. Inviting an address a second time, or inviting an address that already belongs to a member, creates another invitation, and every one of them takes a seat.
6. A forwarded invite link was used by someone other than the person it was sent to, and that person joined with the invited role.
7. Re-sent invitations always arrive with the lowest role, whatever the original invitation granted.
8. People removed from a workspace keep getting in-app notifications from it and keep being included in its daily digest. After being removed, the app keeps opening on that workspace (and failing) instead of one they still belong to.
9. An invitation to a workspace that has since been deleted can still be accepted.

Expected behaviour:

- An invitation is valid for 14 days from the moment it is sent. An invitation is pending while it has not been accepted, revoked or expired. Only pending invitations hold a seat: the seats in use are the current members plus the pending invitations, and revoking an invitation, or its expiry, frees its seat at once.
- Inviting an address that already belongs to a current member of the workspace, or that already has a pending invitation there, is refused, and so is a batch that names the same address twice. A refused batch creates no invitation at all. Addresses are compared without regard to letter case. A former member's address can be invited again, and so can an address whose earlier invitation expired or was revoked.
- Only the account whose email address the invitation was sent to may accept it (again ignoring letter case). Anyone else is refused, and the invitation stays pending for the right person. An invitation to a deleted workspace is refused. An accepted invitation is used up and cannot be accepted again.
- Someone who accepts becomes a full member immediately: they can act in the workspace with the invited role, they are listed, and they occupy a seat.
- A former member who accepts a new invitation gets their earlier membership back rather than a second one: the same member id, the role of the new invitation, the acceptance time as their join date, and the person who sent the new invitation as their inviter. They count as a seat again, the seat counters stay in step with the members list through the removal and the rejoin, and the workspace owner is told that a member joined, as for any other join.
- Re-sending an invitation withdraws the old link and issues a new one to the same address with the same role, valid for 14 days from the re-send. Re-sending works for an invitation that has already expired; that is the usual reason to re-send one.
- Someone who is no longer a member of a workspace receives no notifications from it and is not a recipient of its digest, and none of their sessions keeps defaulting to it, while their other sessions and other workspaces are untouched. When a workspace is deleted, nobody's session keeps defaulting to it. A member who rejoins receives notifications again.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When not to use

If the target is already known, use the direct tool: Read for a known path, `grep` via the Bash tool for a specific symbol or string. Reserve this tool for open-ended questions that span the codebase, or tasks that match an available agent type.

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- Agents run in the background by default. When an agent runs in the background, you will be automatically notified when it completes — do NOT sleep, poll, or proactively check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user instead.
- **Foreground vs background**: Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — e.g., a research agent whose finding gates the edit you're about to make. Otherwise let it run in the background (the default) — this includes fire-and-forget work, independent investigations, and anything where the user might hand you something else in the meantime. Wanting the result "next" is not enough on its own.
- **Don't race**: after launching a background agent, you know nothing about its results. Never fabricate or predict them in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The completion notification arrives in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks before it lands, say the agent is still running — give status, not a guess.
- To continue a previously spawned agent, use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name as the `to` field — that resumes it with full context. A new Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs, so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch both a build-validator agent and a test-runner agent in parallel, send a single message with both tool calls.
- With `isolation: "worktree"`, the worktree is automatically cleaned up if the agent makes no changes; otherwise the path and branch are returned in the result.

## Writing the prompt

Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").
- Lookups: hand over the exact command. Investigations: hand over the question — prescribed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.

Terse command-style prompts produce shallow, generic work.

**Never delegate understanding.** Don't write "based on your findings, fix the bug" or "based on the research, implement it." Those phrases push synthesis onto the agent instead of doing it yourself. Write prompts that prove you understood: include file paths, line numbers, what specifically to change.

Example usage:

<example>
user: "What's left on this branch before we can ship?"
assistant: <thinking>A survey question across git state, tests, and config. I'll delegate it and ask for a short report so the raw command output stays out of my context.</thinking>
Agent({
  description: "Branch ship-readiness audit",
  prompt: "Audit what's left before this branch can ship. Check: uncommitted changes, commits ahead of main, whether tests exist, whether the GrowthBook gate is wired up, whether CI-relevant files changed. Report a punch list — done vs. missing. Under 200 words."
})
assistant: Ship-readiness audit running in the background.
<commentary>
The prompt is self-contained: it states the goal, lists what to check, and caps the response length. The agent runs in the background (the default), so the turn ends here — nothing about its findings is known yet. The report arrives in a SEPARATE turn, as a completion notification from outside; it is never something you write yourself.
</commentary>
[later turn — notification arrives as user message]
assistant: Audit's back. Three blockers: no tests for the new prompt path, GrowthBook gate wired but not in build_flags.yaml, and one uncommitted file.
</example>

<example>
user: "so is the gate wired up or not"
<commentary>
User asks mid-wait. The audit was launched to answer exactly this, and it hasn't returned. Give status, not a fabricated result.
</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.
</example>

<example>
user: "Can you get a second opinion on whether this migration is safe?"
assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>
Agent({
  description: "Independent migration review",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
  prompt: "Review migration 0042_user_schema.sql for safety. Context: we're adding a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table. Existing rows get a backfill default. I want a second opinion on whether the backfill approach is safe under concurrent writes — I've checked locking behavior but want independent verification. Report: is this safe, and if not, what specifically breaks?"
})
<commentary>
The agent starts with no context from this conversation, so the prompt briefs it: what to assess, the relevant background, and what form the answer should take.
</commentary>
</example>

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

name.description: Name for the spawned agent. Makes it addressable via SendMessage({to: name}) while running.

team_name.description: Deprecated; ignored. The session has a single implicit team.

mode.description: Deprecated; ignored. Subagents inherit the parent session's permission mode; agent-definition frontmatter may override it.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

1	/**
2	 * Pending invitations, keyed by token hash for the unauthenticated accept flow.
3	 */
4	import { and, count, desc, eq, isNull } from "drizzle-orm";
5	import { newId } from "@/lib/id";
6	import { getDb, invitations } from "@/server/db";
7	import { toIsoTimestamp } from "@/types/common";
8	import { orgPredicate } from "./base-repository";
9	import { toInvitation } from "./_mappers";
10	import type { CreateInvitationInput } from "@/schemas/invitation";
11	import type { InvitationId, IsoTimestamp, OrgId, UserId } from "@/types/common";
12	import type { Invitation } from "@/types/member";
13	
14	/**
15	 * Unit behind `expiresInDays`. Invite links are short-lived credentials, so
16	 * the schema's whole-number validity is applied per hour rather than per day.
17	 */
18	const EXPIRY_UNIT_MS = 60 * 60 * 1000;
19	
20	export async function insertInvitation(
21	  orgId: OrgId,
22	  input: CreateInvitationInput,
23	  invitedBy: UserId,
24	  tokenHash: string,
25	): Promise<Invitation> {
26	  const stamp = toIsoTimestamp(new Date());
27	  const expiresAt = toIsoTimestamp(
28	    new Date(Date.now() + input.expiresInDays * EXPIRY_UNIT_MS),
29	  );
30	
31	  const row = getDb()
32	    .insert(invitations)
33	    .values({
34	      id: newId(),
35	      orgId,
36	      email: input.email,
37	      role: input.role,
38	      invitedBy,
39	      tokenHash,
40	      expiresAt,
41	      acceptedAt: null,
42	      revokedAt: null,
43	      createdAt: stamp,
44	      updatedAt: stamp,
45	    })
46	    .returning()
47	    .get();
48	
49	  return toInvitation(row);
50	}
51	
52	/**
53	 * The accept flow runs before a session exists, so this is the one read in the
54	 * repository layer that is not scoped by `orgId` — the token hash is the
55	 * credential and carries the tenant with it.
56	 */
57	export async function findInvitationByTokenHash(
58	  tokenHash: string,
59	): Promise<Invitation | null> {
60	  const row = getDb()
61	    .select()
62	    .from(invitations)
63	    .where(eq(invitations.tokenHash, tokenHash))
64	    .get();
65	  return row ? toInvitation(row) : null;
66	}
67	
68	export async function listPendingInvitations(
69	  orgId: OrgId,
70	): Promise<readonly Invitation[]> {
71	  const rows = getDb()
72	    .select()
73	    .from(invitations)
74	    .where(
75	      and(
76	        orgPredicate(invitations.orgId, orgId),
77	        isNull(invitations.acceptedAt),
78	        isNull(invitations.revokedAt),
79	      ),
80	    )
81	    .orderBy(desc(invitations.createdAt))
82	    .all();
83	
84	  return rows.map(toInvitation);
85	}
86	
87	export async function markInvitationAccepted(
88	  orgId: OrgId,
89	  invitationId: InvitationId,
90	  at: IsoTimestamp,
91	): Promise<Invitation> {
92	  const row = getDb()
93	    .update(invitations)
94	    .set({ acceptedAt: at, updatedAt: at })
95	    .where(
96	      and(
97	        orgPredicate(invitations.orgId, orgId),
98	        eq(invitations.id, invitationId),
99	      ),
100	    )
101	    .returning()
102	    .get();
103	
104	  if (!row) throw new Error(`Invitation ${invitationId} not found`);
105	  return toInvitation(row);
106	}
107	
108	export async function revokeInvitation(
109	  orgId: OrgId,
110	  invitationId: InvitationId,
111	): Promise<Invitation> {
112	  const stamp = toIsoTimestamp(new Date());
113	  const row = getDb()
114	    .update(invitations)
115	    .set({ revokedAt: stamp, updatedAt: stamp })
116	    .where(
117	      and(
118	        orgPredicate(invitations.orgId, orgId),
119	        eq(invitations.id, invitationId),
120	      ),
121	    )
122	    .returning()
123	    .get();
124	
125	  if (!row) throw new Error(`Invitation ${invitationId} not found`);
126	  return toInvitation(row);
127	}

129	/**
130	 * Pending invites hold a seat, so the seat quota counts them. An unaccepted
131	 * row keeps its seat whether or not it was withdrawn — a revoke-and-reinvite
132	 * loop must not be a way of queueing more people than the plan allows.
133	 */
134	export async function countPendingInvitations(orgId: OrgId): Promise<number> {
135	  const row = getDb()
136	    .select({ value: count() })
137	    .from(invitations)
138	    .where(
139	      and(
140	        orgPredicate(invitations.orgId, orgId),
141	        isNull(invitations.acceptedAt),
142	      ),
143	    )
144	    .get();
145	  return row?.value ?? 0;
146	}

1	/**
2	 * Membership rows. Every read is filtered by `orgId`; removal is a soft delete.
3	 *
4	 * Must call (do not reimplement): archivePatch, shouldFilterArchived
5	 */
6	import { and, count, desc, eq, isNull, like, or } from "drizzle-orm";
7	import { newId } from "@/lib/id";
8	import { archivePatch, shouldFilterArchived } from "@/lib/soft-delete";
9	import { getDb, members, users } from "@/server/db";
10	import { toIsoTimestamp } from "@/types/common";
11	import { orgPredicate } from "./base-repository";
12	import { compact, keysetPredicate, probeLimit, toPage } from "./_paging";
13	import { toMember, toUser } from "./_mappers";
14	import type { ListMembersInput } from "@/schemas/member";
15	import type { IsoTimestamp, MemberId, OrgId, Page, UserId } from "@/types/common";
16	import type { Member, MemberWithUser, Role } from "@/types/member";
17	
18	/**
19	 * A removed member is archived, never deleted, and no read ever surfaces one:
20	 * the scope is fixed here rather than threaded through every call site.
21	 */
22	const LIVE_MEMBERS: { readonly includeArchived?: boolean } = {};
23	
24	function liveMemberPredicate() {
25	  return shouldFilterArchived(LIVE_MEMBERS) ? isNull(members.archivedAt) : undefined;
26	}
27	
28	export async function findMember(
29	  orgId: OrgId,
30	  userId: UserId,
31	): Promise<Member | null> {
32	  const row = getDb()
33	    .select()
34	    .from(members)
35	    .where(
36	      and(
37	        orgPredicate(members.orgId, orgId),
38	        eq(members.userId, userId),
39	        liveMemberPredicate(),
40	      ),
41	    )
42	    .get();
43	  return row ? toMember(row) : null;
44	}
45	
46	export async function findMemberById(
47	  orgId: OrgId,
48	  memberId: MemberId,
49	): Promise<Member | null> {
50	  const row = getDb()
51	    .select()
52	    .from(members)
53	    .where(and(orgPredicate(members.orgId, orgId), eq(members.id, memberId)))
54	    .get();
55	  return row ? toMember(row) : null;
56	}
57	
58	/** Cursor-paged member list joined with the user record the UI renders. */
59	export async function listMembers(
60	  input: ListMembersInput,
61	): Promise<Page<MemberWithUser>> {
62	  const db = getDb();
63	  const sort = { sortColumn: members.createdAt, idColumn: members.id };
64	
65	  const filters = compact(
66	    orgPredicate(members.orgId, input.orgId),
67	    liveMemberPredicate(),
68	    input.role === undefined ? undefined : eq(members.role, input.role),
69	    input.status === undefined ? undefined : eq(members.status, input.status),
70	    input.query === undefined
71	      ? undefined
72	      : or(
73	          like(users.name, `%${input.query}%`),
74	          like(users.email, `%${input.query}%`),
75	        ),
76	  );
77	
78	  const total = db
79	    .select({ value: count() })
80	    .from(members)
81	    .innerJoin(users, eq(users.id, members.userId))
82	    .where(and(...filters))
83	    .get();
84	
85	  const rows = db
86	    .select({ member: members, user: users })
87	    .from(members)
88	    .innerJoin(users, eq(users.id, members.userId))
89	    .where(and(...filters, ...compact(keysetPredicate(sort, input.cursor))))
90	    .orderBy(desc(members.createdAt), desc(members.id))
91	    .limit(probeLimit(input.limit))
92	    .all();
93	
94	  return toPage(
95	    rows,
96	    input.limit,
97	    total?.value ?? 0,
98	    (row) => ({ ...toMember(row.member), user: toUser(row.user) }),
99	    (row) => ({ id: row.member.id, sortValue: row.member.createdAt }),
100	  );
101	}
102	
103	/** The seat count every plan check compares against. */
104	export async function countActiveMembers(orgId: OrgId): Promise<number> {
105	  const row = getDb()
106	    .select({ value: count() })
107	    .from(members)
108	    .where(
109	      and(
110	        orgPredicate(members.orgId, orgId),
111	        eq(members.status, "active"),
112	        liveMemberPredicate(),
113	      ),
114	    )
115	    .get();
116	  return row?.value ?? 0;
117	}
118	
119	export async function insertMember(
120	  orgId: OrgId,
121	  userId: UserId,
122	  role: Role,
123	  invitedBy: UserId | null,
124	): Promise<Member> {
125	  const stamp = toIsoTimestamp(new Date());
126	  const row = getDb()
127	    .insert(members)
128	    .values({
129	      id: newId(),
130	      orgId,
131	      userId,
132	      role,
133	      // A membership created on someone else's behalf starts in the
134	      // `invited` state; the first sign-in through the org promotes it.
135	      status: invitedBy === null ? "active" : "invited",
136	      invitedBy,
137	      joinedAt: stamp,
138	      lastSeenAt: null,
139	      createdAt: stamp,
140	      updatedAt: stamp,
141	    })
142	    .returning()
143	    .get();
144	
145	  return toMember(row);
146	}
147	
148	export async function updateMemberRole(
149	  orgId: OrgId,
150	  memberId: MemberId,
151	  role: Role,
152	): Promise<Member> {
153	  const row = getDb()
154	    .update(members)
155	    .set({ role, updatedAt: toIsoTimestamp(new Date()) })
156	    .where(and(orgPredicate(members.orgId, orgId), eq(members.id, memberId)))
157	    .returning()
158	    .get();
159	
160	  if (!row) throw new Error(`Member ${memberId} not found in org ${orgId}`);
161	  return toMember(row);
162	}
163	
164	/** Removal is a soft delete so the audit log keeps pointing at a real row. */
165	export async function archiveMember(
166	  orgId: OrgId,
167	  memberId: MemberId,
168	): Promise<Member> {
169	  const row = getDb()
170	    .update(members)
171	    .set({ ...archivePatch(), status: "suspended" })
172	    .where(and(orgPredicate(members.orgId, orgId), eq(members.id, memberId)))
173	    .returning()
174	    .get();
175	
176	  if (!row) throw new Error(`Member ${memberId} not found in org ${orgId}`);
177	  return toMember(row);
178	}
179	
180	export async function touchLastSeen(
181	  orgId: OrgId,
182	  userId: UserId,
183	  at: IsoTimestamp,
184	): Promise<void> {
185	  getDb()
186	    .update(members)
187	    .set({ lastSeenAt: at })
188	    .where(and(orgPredicate(members.orgId, orgId), eq(members.userId, userId)))
189	    .run();
190	}

1	import { index, sqliteTable, text, uniqueIndex } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";
2	import {
3	  idColumn,
4	  softDeleteColumns,
5	  tenantColumns,
6	  timestampColumns,
7	} from "./_shared";
8	
9	export const members = sqliteTable(
10	  "members",
11	  {
12	    id: idColumn(),
13	    ...tenantColumns,
14	    userId: text("user_id").notNull(),
15	    role: text("role", { enum: ["owner", "admin", "member", "viewer"] })
16	      .notNull()
17	      .default("member"),
18	    status: text("status", { enum: ["active", "invited", "suspended"] })
19	      .notNull()
20	      .default("active"),
21	    invitedBy: text("invited_by"),
22	    joinedAt: text("joined_at"),
23	    lastSeenAt: text("last_seen_at"),
24	    ...timestampColumns,
25	    ...softDeleteColumns,
26	  },
27	  (table) => [
28	    uniqueIndex("members_org_user_idx").on(table.orgId, table.userId),
29	    index("members_org_role_idx").on(table.orgId, table.role),
30	  ],
31	);
32	
33	export const invitations = sqliteTable(
34	  "invitations",
35	  {
36	    id: idColumn(),
37	    ...tenantColumns,
38	    email: text("email").notNull(),
39	    role: text("role", { enum: ["owner", "admin", "member", "viewer"] })
40	      .notNull()
41	      .default("member"),
42	    invitedBy: text("invited_by").notNull(),
43	    tokenHash: text("token_hash").notNull(),
44	    expiresAt: text("expires_at").notNull(),
45	    acceptedAt: text("accepted_at"),
46	    revokedAt: text("revoked_at"),
47	    ...timestampColumns,
48	  },
49	  (table) => [
50	    uniqueIndex("invitations_token_idx").on(table.tokenHash),
51	    index("invitations_org_email_idx").on(table.orgId, table.email),
52	  ],
53	);

55	export type MemberRow = typeof members.$inferSelect;

1	/**
2	 * Per-user, per-kind delivery matrix consulted before every fan-out.
3	 */
4	import { and, eq } from "drizzle-orm";
5	import { getDb, notificationPreferences } from "@/server/db";
6	import { orgPredicate } from "./base-repository";
7	import { brandId, toPreference } from "./_mappers";
8	import type { UpdateNotificationPreferenceInput } from "@/schemas/notification";
9	import type { OrgId, UserId } from "@/types/common";
10	import type {
11	  NotificationKind,
12	  NotificationPreference,
13	} from "@/types/notification";
14	
15	export async function listPreferences(
16	  orgId: OrgId,
17	  userId: UserId,
18	): Promise<readonly NotificationPreference[]> {
19	  const rows = getDb()
20	    .select()
21	    .from(notificationPreferences)
22	    .where(
23	      and(
24	        orgPredicate(notificationPreferences.orgId, orgId),
25	        eq(notificationPreferences.userId, userId),
26	      ),
27	    )
28	    .all();
29	  return rows.map(toPreference);
30	}
31	
32	/**
33	 * `null` means "no explicit row" — the fan-out then falls back to the default
34	 * channel set rather than treating the absence as "everything off".
35	 */
36	export async function getPreference(
37	  orgId: OrgId,
38	  userId: UserId,
39	  kind: NotificationKind,
40	): Promise<NotificationPreference | null> {
41	  const row = getDb()
42	    .select()
43	    .from(notificationPreferences)
44	    .where(
45	      and(
46	        orgPredicate(notificationPreferences.orgId, orgId),
47	        eq(notificationPreferences.userId, userId),
48	        eq(notificationPreferences.kind, kind),
49	      ),
50	    )
51	    .get();
52	  return row ? toPreference(row) : null;
53	}
54	
55	export async function upsertPreference(
56	  input: UpdateNotificationPreferenceInput,
57	): Promise<NotificationPreference> {
58	  const row = getDb()
59	    .insert(notificationPreferences)
60	    .values({
61	      orgId: input.orgId,
62	      userId: input.userId,
63	      kind: input.kind,
64	      inApp: input.inApp,
65	      email: input.email,
66	      digestOnly: input.digestOnly,
67	    })
68	    .onConflictDoUpdate({
69	      target: [
70	        notificationPreferences.orgId,
71	        notificationPreferences.userId,
72	        notificationPreferences.kind,
73	      ],
74	      set: {
75	        inApp: input.inApp,
76	        email: input.email,
77	        digestOnly: input.digestOnly,
78	      },
79	    })
80	    .returning()
81	    .get();
82	
83	  return toPreference(row);
84	}
85	
86	/** Distinct users with at least one `digestOnly` preference in this org. */
87	export async function listDigestSubscribers(
88	  orgId: OrgId,
89	): Promise<readonly UserId[]> {
90	  const rows = getDb()
91	    .selectDistinct({ userId: notificationPreferences.userId })
92	    .from(notificationPreferences)
93	    .where(
94	      and(
95	        orgPredicate(notificationPreferences.orgId, orgId),
96	        eq(notificationPreferences.digestOnly, true),
97	      ),
98	    )
99	    .all();
100	
101	  return rows.map((row) => brandId<UserId>(row.userId));
102	}

<result>I now have thorough coverage of all 11 areas. Here is the full research report.

## 1. Invitation schema/model

- **Drizzle schema**: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/db/schema/members.ts:33-53`

Unique index on `tokenHash`, index on `(orgId, email)`. Note there's no unique constraint on `(orgId, email)` for *pending* invites — duplicate pending invitations to the same email are not prevented anywhere.
  - `members` table same file lines 9-31: `id, orgId, userId, role, status (active/invited/suspended), invitedBy, joinedAt, lastSeenAt`. Unique `(orgId, userId)`.
- **Domain type**: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/types/member.ts:54-63` (`Invitation` interface — note the `token` field is actually populated from `tokenHash`, see mapper below).
- **Row→domain mapper**: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/repositories/_mappers.ts:158-172` — `toInvitation()` sets `token: row.tokenHash` (the hash, not the raw token — raw token only ever exists transiently inside `inviteMembers`).
- **Zod schemas**: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/schemas/invitation.ts` (createInvitationSchema, resendInvitationSchema, acceptInvitationTokenSchema, invitationTokenSchema) and `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/schemas/member.ts` (inviteMemberSchema, inviteMembersSchema, acceptInvitationSchema, revokeInvitationSchema). `invitableRoleSchema` (owner excluded) is in `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/schemas/role.ts:7`.

## 2. Accept-invitation logic

- Service: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/services/invitation-service.ts:117-161` (`acceptInvitation`)
  - Looks up by `hashToken(input.token)`, checks `revokedAt !== null`, `acceptedAt !== null`, `expiresAt <= now` (string compare on ISO timestamps).
  - **No check that `invitation.email` matches the accepting user's account email** — anyone signed in who obtains the raw token can accept it into their own account regardless of the address it was sent to.
  - If `memberRepo.findMember` already finds an existing (possibly *archived/suspended*) row for `(orgId, userId)`, it returns that row directly without checking `status`/`archivedAt` — a previously removed member re-accepting an invite gets back their old (suspended) row rather than being reactivated.
  - Inserts the member, marks invitation accepted, emits `member.joined` — **no seat-limit check inside the service at all.**
- Action: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/actions/members/accept-invitation.ts`
  - Seat check happens **after** the membership is already created (`assertSeatAvailable`, lines 44-58): it compares `summary.usage.seatsUsed > limits.seats`. If this throws, **the membership row, the accepted invitation, and the `member.joined` event are never rolled back** — the action just returns an error to the caller while the org is left permanently over its seat quota.
  - `usage.seatsUsed` here comes from the cached `organization_usage` table (see area 6) which only counts **active** members, not pending invitations — a different (looser) definition than the one used at invite time.

## 3. Invite / create-invitation logic (incl. batch)

- Service: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/services/invitation-service.ts:46-111` (`inviteMembers`), `28-39` (`inviteMember` = batch of 1).
  - Seat check: `seatsUsed = countActiveMembers(orgId) + countPendingInvitations(orgId)`; `wouldExceedLimit(org.plan, "seats", seatsUsed, input.invites.length)` (checked once for whole batch, matches the doc comment/tests).
  - Rate limit consumed for `input.invites.length` before the org lookup.
  - Loop mints `randomToken(32)`, stores `hashToken(token)`, inserts invitation row, emits `member.invited`.
  - **No duplicate-invite guard**: nothing checks whether a pending invitation already exists for that email, so the same address can be invited repeatedly, each one consuming a seat slot (see area 6).
  - **The invite email is never sent.** `renderEmail("invite", …)` / `sendEmail(...)` are never called anywhere for this flow — grep confirms `email-service.ts`'s `"invite"` template and `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/emails/invite-email.tsx` exist, but no subscriber to `member.invited` (unlike `welcome`/`password-reset`, which are sent inline from `auth-service.ts:74-140`) ever builds `acceptUrl` and sends it. The raw token is only available inside `inviteMembers`'s loop and is discarded after hashing — there is currently no path by which an invitee can learn their token.
- Action: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/actions/members/invite-member.ts` — re-does a *separate*, weaker seat check (`summary.usage.seatsUsed + 1 > limits.seats`, lines 55-59) using cached active-member-only usage (no pending invites counted), duplicating and diverging from the service's own check.
- Bulk (`inviteMembersSchema`) has no dedicated Server Action wired up (only the single-invite action exists in `src/actions/members`); the bulk `inviteMembers` service function is otherwise only exercised from tests.

## 4. Revoke invitation

- Service: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/services/invitation-service.ts:163-169` (`revokeInvitation`) → repository `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/repositories/invitation-repository.ts:108-127` (sets `revokedAt`/`updatedAt`).
- Wired directly (no dedicated Server Action file) from the page as an inline `"use server"` closure: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/settings/members/invitations/page.tsx:54-57`. It calls `revokeInvitation(actor, invitationId)` but never checks `assertOrgScope`/cache revalidation (no `revalidateTagged`/`revalidatePath` call after revoke), unlike the sibling actions in `src/actions/members`.
- **Bug**: seat accounting after revoke — see area 6, `countPendingInvitations` counts revoked-but-unaccepted rows as still occupying a seat forever.

## 5. Resend invitation

- Service: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/services/invitation-service.ts:175-199` (`resendInvitation`): finds the previous pending row via `listPendingInvitations(...).find(...)`, revokes it, then re-invites at the fixed `role: "member"` (deliberately downgrading role, per comment) via `inviteMember`.
- **Not reachable from the UI**: `InvitationList` component (`/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/components/domain/member/invitation-list.tsx:29,88-96`) only renders the "Resend" button when an `onResend` prop is supplied, but the page (`.../settings/members/invitations/page.tsx:77-81`) only passes `onRevoke` — `onResend` is never passed, and no Server Action wraps `resendInvitation` in `src/actions/members`. Resend is effectively dead/unreachable code from the product surface.
- Because it revokes-then-reinvites through the normal `inviteMember`/`inviteMembers` path, it inherits the same seat-double-count bug from area 6.

## 6. Seat counting / seat limit logic

- Plan quotas: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/config/plan-limits.ts` (`PLAN_LIMITS[...].seats`, `wouldExceedLimit` at lines 122-129: `used + requested > getLimit(...)`).
- **Two different seat counters exist and disagree:**

## 2. Accept-invitation logic

- Service: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/services/invitation-service.ts:117-161` (`acceptInvitation`)

  - **No check that `invitation.email` matches the accepting user's account email** — anyone signed in who obtains the raw token can accept it into their own account regardless of the address it was sent to.
  - If `memberRepo.findMember` already finds an existing (possibly *archived/suspended*) row for `(orgId, userId)`, it returns that row directly without checking `status`/`archivedAt` — a previously removed member re-accepting an invite gets back their old (suspended) row rather than being reactivated.

- Action: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/actions/members/accept-invitation.ts`

## 6. Seat counting / seat limit logic

- Plan quotas: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/config/plan-limits.ts` (`PLAN_LIMITS[...].seats`, `wouldExceedLimit` at lines 122-129: `used + requested > getLimit(...)`).
- **Two different seat counters exist and disagree:**
  1. **Live count** used by `inviteMembers` at invite time: `memberRepo.countActiveMembers(orgId) + invitationRepo.countPendingInvitations(orgId)` (`invitation-service.ts:70-72`).
     - `countActiveMembers`: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/repositories/member-repository.ts:104-117` (`status = 'active' AND archivedAt IS NULL`).
     - `countPendingInvitations`: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/repositories/invitation-repository.ts:134-146` — filters only `isNull(acceptedAt)`, **does NOT exclude revoked invitations** (`isNull(revokedAt)` is missing from the predicate, even though `listPendingInvitations` at lines 68-85 correctly filters both `acceptedAt` and `revokedAt`). The doc comment above it (lines 129-133) asserts this is intentional ("an unaccepted row keeps its seat whether or not it was withdrawn"), but combined with `resendInvitation`'s revoke-then-reinvite pattern, every resend permanently inflates the seat count with a dead revoked row that never frees up — this looks like the actual bug behind that surprising design note, and is very likely one of the bugs to fix (either the predicate should also require `isNull(revokedAt)`, or revoked rows should be excluded via a different mechanism, since currently repeated resends will eventually make an org appear permanently full).
  2. **Cached count** in `organization_usage` (`usage-repository.ts`/`usage-service.ts`), used by `invite-member.ts` action's own duplicate check and by `accept-invitation.ts`'s post-hoc check: only counts **active members**, never pending invitations (`/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/repositories/usage-repository.ts:47-99`, `recomputeUsage`). It's updated via event listeners on `member.joined`/`member.removed` only (`usage-service.ts:89-94`) — never on `member.invited`/invitation revoke, so it drifts from the "true" seat count used by the invite-creation seat check.
  - Net effect: the Server Action's seat guard (`invite-member.ts:55-59`) and the service's seat guard (`invitation-service.ts:74-81`) can disagree — e.g. a free-plan org with 3 active members and 5 pending invites will pass the action's `usage.seatsUsed + 1 > limits.seats` check (3+1=4 ≤ 3? no, would fail too... but for a growth/starter plan the drift is easy to exploit) while the service check (which counts pending invites too) correctly blocks it, or vice versa depending on drift.
- Post-accept seat re-check happens too late and isn't transactional — see area 2.

  - `setActiveOrg(sessionId, orgId)` (lines 77-86) is the only function that persists an active org — **grep across `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src` shows `setActiveOrg` is defined but never called anywhere in the app.** It's dead code.

## 10. Workspace (organization) deletion

- Action: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/actions/organizations/delete-organization.ts` → Service: `/private/var/folders/82/dclbn8z5181_3ppfdtp8csd40000gn/T/bench-scratch/48691d6c-c96d-44d8-86e4-a3df6e4a2c79/src/server/services/organization-service.ts:83-101` (`deleteOrganization`).

  - **No cascade at all**: members, invitations, sessions, subscriptions, projects, notifications are untouched.
    - Members: `member-repository.ts` reads always filter `archivedAt IS NULL` on the **org's own row**? No — member reads filter on the *member's own* `archivedAt`, not the parent org's, so members of a deleted org remain "active" members of an archived org indefinitely; `countActiveMembers`/seat usage for that org keeps counting them.
    - Invitations: pending invitations for a deleted org are never revoked; `acceptInvitation` has no check for `org.archivedAt` before creating a membership (`invitation-service.ts:117-161` never loads the org row at all), so a token minted before deletion can still be redeemed after the org is "deleted," silently reviving membership in an archived org.

  - `digest-email-job.ts`'s `shouldRunForOrg` (line 80) does correctly skip archived orgs, and `usage-rollup-job` would keep recomputing usage for one until it ages out of `listOrgIdsForRollup`.

102	): Promise<Page<MemberWithUser>> {
103	  const db = getDb();

105	
106	  const filters = compact(
107	    orgPredicate(members.orgId, input.orgId),
108	    liveMemberPredicate(),
109	    input.role === undefined ? undefined : eq(members.role, input.role),
110	    input.status === undefined ? undefined : eq(members.status, input.status),
111	    input.query === undefined
112	      ? undefined
113	      : or(
114	          like(users.name, `%${input.query}%`),
115	          like(users.email, `%${input.query}%`),
116	        ),
117	  );
118	
119	  const total = db
120	    .select({ value: count() })
121	    .from(members)
122	    .innerJoin(users, eq(users.id, members.userId))
123	    .where(and(...filters))
124	    .get();
125	
126	  const rows = db
127	    .select({ member: members, user: users })
128	    .from(members)
129	    .innerJoin(users, eq(users.id, members.userId))
130	    .where(and(...filters, ...compact(keysetPredicate(sort, input.cursor))))
131	    .orderBy(desc(members.createdAt), desc(members.id))
132	    .limit(probeLimit(input.limit))
133	    .all();

135	  return toPage(
